### **Introduction**

GitHub is a cloud-based service for storing and sharing source code. Using GitHub with Visual Studio Code lets you share your source code and collaborate with others right within your editor. There are many ways to interact with GitHub, for example, via their website or the Git command-line interface (CLI), but in VS Code, the rich GitHub integration is provided by the GitHub Pull Requests and Issues extension. 

In Part 1 of this module, you learned about Version Control, the differences between Git and GitHub, and the Basic Git Workflow. 

Now, in this module, we'll perform and use GitHub as Version Control, use Git Commands without leaving the Visual Code Studio for Collaboration.

### **Module Learning Objectives**

1. To perform Pull Requests, Code Reviews, Recovery, and Rollback of your codes  
2. To collaborate with at least one teammate using VS Code, Git, and GitHub by contributing to a shared project, resolving conflicts, and communicating effectively with teammates.  
3. To be able to turn data into visuals, it helps identify trends, patterns, and outliers, allowing for faster, data-driven decisions.

#### **1.1. Setting up Prerequisites (10mins)**

To get started with GitHub in VS Code, you need to have:

* installed VS Code,  
* installed Git on your computer,  
  * Recheck if you have configured the username and email that Git will use when you commit changes. *(You have probably configured it already in the previous module)*  
    * To check, type in your terminal as follows, and it will show your details

    ![][image1]

    * If not yet configured, then type in your terminal the following command and details, then you may check again.  
      * **git config –global user.name “Your Name”**  
      * **git config –global user.email “your.email@example.com”**  
          
* created a GitHub account, and  
* installed the GitHub Pull Requests extension in VS Code

#### **1.2. GitHub Collaboration (60mins)**

After learning the Basic Git workflow in the previous module, like cloning a repository, committing changes, and pushing and pulling updates to and from our VS Code Editor to local (computer) and remote repository, which is GitHub, this time let us simulate real-world software development by collaborating with others on a project.

***1.2.1 Pull Changes vs Pull Requests***  
First, let us see the differences between **pulling changes** (`git pull`) and working with a **Pull Request**. A `git pull` is a command that immediately updates your local repository by fetching and merging changes from a remote repository. In contrast, a pull request (PR) does not automatically affect your local repository \- it is a collaboration tool used to propose and review changes. The updates from a PR only appear in your local repository after you manually run a Git command to fetch those changes.

See the summary of differences as shown in the table below.

| Feature | git pull | Pull Request |
| ----- | ----- | ----- |
| **Type** | A Git command |  A GitHub (or GitLab, Bitbucket) feature/process |
| **Direction** | Pulls changes *from* a remote repo *to* your local repo | Requests an administrator to pull changes *from* your repo *into* their main repo |
| **Purpose** | To synchronize and update your local codebase | To propose changes, facilitate code review, and discuss modifications before merging |
| **Workflow** | An automated command-line action | An interactive process involving a web interface, discussion, and approval |

***1.2.2. Understanding Pull Request (PR), Code Reviews , Recovery and Roll Back![][image3]***

***GIF by** [Brij kishore Pandey](https://www.linkedin.com/in/brijpandeyji?trk=public_post_comment-text)*

Here is a brief description and purpose of each action:

| Concept | Description | When it takes Place | Who initiates it |
| ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| **Pull Request (PR)** | A request to add your changes to the main project, allowing teammates to review, discuss, and approve changes before merging to ensure quality and consistency | After completing a feature, fix update, and before merging into the main branch | The developer who made the changes |
| **Code Reviews** | The process of checking someone else’s code before it is accepted, helping identify errors, improving code quality, and ensuring standards are followed | After a pull request is submitted and before it is merged | Assigned reviewers, teammates, or senior developers |
| **Recovery** | The process of restoring lost or deleted work, such as files or commits, to recover from accidental deletion or errors | When files or commits are accidentally lost, deleted, or corrupted | A developer or user who needs to restore the work |
| **Roll Back** | The act of returning the project to a previous stable version to fix issues caused by recent changes | When a new update introduces bugs, errors, or system failures | Developer, team lead, or system administrator |

After Learning the Basic Git Workflow and various actions with GitHub, here is a full course on Git and GitHub which might help you better understand how collaboration works. In this video, you will be able to grasp the summary of all **WH** questions about Git and GitHub.

Disclaimer: This video uses WebStorm (WS) instead of Visual Studio Code (VS Code) and demonstrates Git commands through the terminal instead of the built-in editor features like  those in VS Code. It would be great if you could check the correlation between the terminal commands and their counterparts in VS Code, as presented in the previous ILA Task. You may also reflect on why we will be using VS Code Editor over WebStorm (WS).

**Learning Resource: Videos on the [Full Course of Git and GitHub](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=S7XpTAnSDL4)**

Also in this video, you might wonder what .gitignore and readme.md. Let's take a look at what they are.

* A **.gitignore** file is used to specify which files and folders Git should ignore and not track in a repository. This is useful for excluding unnecessary or sensitive files, such as system files or configuration files. *(Feel free to explore how to create a .gitignore file.)*  
* On the other hand,  a **README.md** file in a GitHub repository that is **markdown**\-formatted and serves as the project's primary documentation and introduction. It is the first thing visitors see on the repository's main page as its contents are automatically displayed below the repository's file list. It provides essential information about the project, such as its purpose, setup instructions, and usage. To learn how to effectively write a .md file, you may refer to Github’s documentation on basic formatting syntax.

	  
	**Learning Resource: Documentation on [Basic Writing and Formatting](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/writing-on-github/getting-started-with-writing-and-formatting-on-github/basic-writing-and-formatting-syntax)**

#### **1.3 Collaborative GitHub Workflow Activity**

| Blend ILA Pair Activity: Collaborative GitHub Workflow (20mins in class and 30mins ILA).  This Activity may be continued during ILA if unfinished in the classroom setting.  Learning Objectives By the end of this activity, learners will be able to: Collaborate using a shared GitHub repository Use branches, commits, and pull requests Review a partner’s code and resolve merge conflicts Grouping Students work in pairs Roles: Developer A and Developer B (swap roles halfway) Tools Required VS Code Git installed locally Account and Access to GitHub Activity Scenario You and your partner are collaborating on a small project: A simple README-driven project (e.g., “Study Tips for Programming” or “Beginner Git Commands”). Step-by-Step Instructions Part 1: Repository Setup Developer A creates a new GitHub repository. Add a README.md with a project title and short description (primarily answers the what, why, and how of the project like *“What problem does it solve?”*). Invite Developer B as a collaborator. Both partners clone the repository locally. Part 2: Branching & Individual Work  Developer A: Create a branch called feature-tips Add a section to the README (e.g., “Git Best Practices”) Developer B: Create a branch called feature-resources Add a section (e.g., “Helpful Learning Resources”) Each partner: Commit changes with a clear commit message Push their branch to GitHub Part 3: Pull Requests & Code Review  Each partner opens a Pull Request (PR) from their branch to main. Review your partner’s PR: Leave at least one comment Suggest one improvement (wording, formatting, clarity) Make requested changes if needed. Approve and merge the PR. Part 4: Conflict Practice Both partners edit the same line in README.md on separate branches. Attempt to merge both PRs. Resolve the merge conflict together and commit the fix. Class Forum: Graded to be submitted in KHUB Refer to the following questions to write a reflection regarding your process: Do you experience conflicts? What steps helped avoid merge conflicts? How did code review improve the final result? What was challenging about collaborating with Git and GitHub?  |

### **Closing/ Summary/ Key takeaways**

* Today, you worked together in groups to plan a project and use GitHub to organize your ideas.  
* You learned how to create a repository, add a README, and work as a team to edit and update your project plan.  
* Collaboration means sharing ideas, listening to each other, and solving problems together.  
* Using Github helps you keep track of changes and makes teamwork easier.
